title: Unleashing Kid Wizards
author: Stefan Bauschard
summary: Stefan Bauschard describes an AI summer camp program for middle school students that uses Google AI Studio to teach children to build working applications, create AI-assisted stories, and design interactive tools -- all without framing any of it as 'using AI to cheat.' The piece documents specific student projects: a game that teaches younger kids their multiplication tables, a story generator that asks for the reader's favorite animal and builds a narrative around it, and a homework-help tutor for a sibling with dyslexia. Bauschard argues that the middle school age range is the ideal entry point for serious AI education: old enough to have authentic problems worth solving, young enough that the 'this is how things have always been done' resistance has not yet calcified. The camp uses a specific pedagogical model: no templates, no cheating frames, just 'here is a problem you care about, here is a powerful tool, figure out how to use the tool to solve the problem.' The piece documents what this looks like in practice and what it produces.
points: * Middle school is the ideal AI education entry point: students are old enough to have authentic problems worth solving and young enough that resistance to new approaches has not calcified. * The no-template, no-cheating-frame pedagogy -- 'here is a problem you care about, here is a powerful tool' -- produces qualitatively different engagement from structured AI tutorials that specify both the tool and the task. * Google AI Studio is accessible enough for middle schoolers with no prior programming experience to build working applications in a single camp session, lowering the barrier between problem identification and functional solution. * Student projects document genuine problem-solving motivation: a multiplication table game for younger siblings, a dyslexia-tutor for a sibling, a story generator built around reader-specified inputs -- all driven by authentic care for a real user. * The camp model demonstrates that 'AI literacy' at this age level is not about understanding AI technically but about developing the disposition to identify problems, imagine AI-assisted solutions, and iterate toward working implementations.
quotes: We don't tell them they're learning AI. We tell them they have a problem and we have a tool. The problem has to be real -- something they actually care about, something that affects them or someone they love. The tool is Google AI Studio. The rest is theirs.

One student built a multiplication tutor for her younger brother in about three hours. She had never programmed before. She had never heard of an API. She had a brother who struggled with math and a three-hour block of time and a very clear sense of what she wanted it to do. That was enough.

The cheating frame is the enemy of real AI education. When you teach kids that AI is the thing you use instead of doing the work, you've taught them something false and damaging. AI is a tool for doing harder work than you could do without it. The camp is designed around that premise.

Middle schoolers are the right age for this. They're old enough to have real problems -- a sibling who needs help, a concept they can't explain to a friend, a game they want to exist but doesn't. They're young enough that 'this is how things are done' hasn't locked them into thinking there's only one way to approach a problem.

What we're watching is a generation of kids develop a fundamentally different relationship to problem-solving. They don't ask 'can I do this?' They ask 'what tool do I need?' That shift in the framing of capability is what we're trying to produce, and we're watching it happen.
